rationale: Based on 22 months of ethnographic fieldwork in Mumbai (qualitative design), Anand (2012) examines how Muslim residents in Premnagar—despite many holding pre-1995 recognized settlement status—are disconnected from reliable municipal water through street-level bureaucratic discretion and informal workarounds (discretion_accommodation). Municipal water engineers selectively neglect maintenance, judge complainants' legitimacy, and gatekeep complaints behind paid-bill proofs, while licensed/informal plumbers mediate access through unauthorized connections and negotiated compromises. Secondary rule mechanisms discussed include formal documentation/ID and licensed-plumber requirements and arduous billing/complaint steps (procedural_burden, eligibility_status_documentation, review_redress), estimated billing without subsidies (fees_tariffs_subsidies), and periodic raids/cutoffs of unauthorized pipes (enforcement_sanctions). Outcomes span co-equally central dimensions (multiple), led by effective_access (rusted/dry mains, low pressure, 4:30 AM collection schedules, gendered fetching burdens, and reliance on sewage-contaminated unpotable borewells) alongside primary_connection (shift from formal municipal hookups to unauthorized plumber connections and borewell networks), administrative_outcome (refusal/delay of complaints and applications), and economic_access (high repeated connection payments to plumbers and estimated bills for dry lines).
